exercise.py: Dào bù tóng, bù xiāng wéi móu.
exercise.en: Those whose ways differ do not make plans together.
exercise.tests: 同
exercise.h_s: 道不同，不相为谋。

lessons.culture: The story is a weapon in a debate. Han Fei's opponents praised both Yao and Shun as perfect sage-kings; Han Fei answers that if Shun had to correct Yao's mistakes, Yao wasn't perfect, and if Yao was perfect, Shun had nothing to correct: "you cannot praise both". The word 矛盾 entered modern Chinese (and Japanese, *mujun*) as the standard term for "contradiction", including the Marxist "contradiction" of Mao's essay 《矛盾論》.

lessons.title: 揠苗助長
lessons.title_en: Pulling Up the Sprouts to Help Them Grow

source.author: 孟子 Mencius (c. 372–289 BC)
source.text_from: 《孟子·公孫丑上》, as quoted on Wiktionary 揠苗助長 (CC BY-SA); lines 1–7 also match the Hong Kong EDB edition.

lessons.intro: Mencius, the second great Confucian, is explaining to a disciple how to nourish one's "flood-like qi" (浩然之氣), the moral courage that grows from always doing what is right. You can't force it, he says, and you mustn't neglect it either, and he tells this story of yet another man of Song. New in this lesson: the particle 矣, which marks something that *has happened* or *has become* the case, and the reading 長 zhǎng "to grow".

lines.h: 宋人有閔其苗之不長而揠之者，
lines.py: Sòng rén yǒu mǐn qí miáo zhī bù zhǎng ér yà zhī zhě,
lines.en: There was a man of Song who, worried that his sprouts weren't growing, tugged at them.
lines.lit: Song people there-was worried his sprouts' not growing and pulled them one
lines.h_s: 宋人有闵其苗之不长而揠之者，

lines.en: He came home, worn out,
and said to his family:
"I'm exhausted today:
I've been helping the sprouts grow!"

lines.py: Qí zǐ qū ér wǎng shì zhī,
lines.en: His son hurried off to look at them;
the sprouts had withered.

lines.h: 天下之不助苗長者寡矣。
lines.py: Tiān xià zhī bù zhù miáo zhǎng zhě guǎ yǐ.
lines.en: In this world, few are those who don't help their sprouts grow.
lines.h_s: 天下之不助苗长者寡矣。

lines.py: Yǐ wéi wú yì ér shě zhī zhě,
lines.en: Those who think it's no use and leave them alone
are those who don't weed their sprouts;
those who help them grow
are those who tug at their sprouts.
Not only is that no use —
it actually harms them.

notes.text: A long first line, built like L1's 宋人有耕者: 宋人 **有** [ … ] **者** "among the people of Song there was one who …" (→ L1 n.2). Inside the brackets: 閔 mǐn "to worry about" (later written 憫) + its object 其苗之不長 "his sprouts' not growing", the subject + 之 + predicate pattern of → L2 n.3. Then 而揠之 "and pulled at them" (→ L1 n.4, L2 n.2).

**長** has two readings. zhǎng = "to grow; to be the elder, to lead"; cháng = "long". Here, and in the idiom 揠苗助長, it is zhǎng. Chinese often marks a change of word by a change of tone or initial (破音字); the dictionary entry for 長 lists them separately.

**-然** rán turns a word into a description of manner: 芒芒然 "in a weary way, worn out". 芒芒 is a reduplicated descriptive word; commentators gloss it as 疲倦的樣子 "looking tired". You'll meet many ~然 words: 忽然, 果然 and 自然 all come from this pattern.
**謂 A 曰** "said to A": 謂 takes the person spoken to as its object. **其人** here is "his household, his family". Compare L2 n.8, where 其人 meant "that man": context decides.

**病** = "exhausted, worn out", not "ill" (古今詞義 → L1 n.3). In early texts 疾 is the ordinary word for illness and 病 a *serious* illness or extreme fatigue. **矣** yǐ marks a new situation: "I'm (now) exhausted". 也 states what *is* (→ L1 n.11); 矣 states what *has come to be*. The story turns on three 矣 (lines 4, 5 and 7): he is tired now, the sprouts have been "helped", and by then they have withered.
**予** yú = "I, me". Classical Chinese has several first-person pronouns: 吾 (L2), 我, 予/余. Here the farmer is boasting.
**趨** qū "to hurry, walk fast" — the middle gear between 行 "walk" and 走 "run" (→ L1 n.3). **往** "to go (to)", **視** "to look at". 而 again links the manner to the action.
**則** zé "then, and so": here it marks what the son *found*: "the sprouts — (by then) they had withered". 槁 gǎo "dried up, withered".

notes.at: 天下之不助苗長者寡矣
notes.text: Mencius turns to the moral. The subject is a long 者-phrase: 天下之 [不助苗長] 者 "those in the world who don't help their sprouts grow", and the predicate is 寡矣 "are few". **寡** guǎ "few" (its opposite is 眾). In other words: almost everyone forces things.
notes.at_s: 天下之不助苗长者寡矣

notes.text: **以為** yǐ wéi "to think, consider that". Here it introduces a whole clause: 以為無益 "think it is no use". (In L6 you will see 以 A 為 B "regard A as B" split around its object.) **捨** shě "to give up, leave alone" (also written 舍).

**A 者，B 者也** — the classic definition sentence: "A is B". Both halves are 者 phrases ("those who …"), and 也 closes the judgment (→ L1 n.11). Lines 9–12 give two of them in parallel: neglecting = not weeding; forcing = tugging.
**非徒 … 而又 …** "not only … but also …". 非 fēi negates a whole statement or a noun ("it is not that …"), whereas 不 negates a verb. 徒 tú "merely, only". 害 "to harm".

glossary.en: final particle: new situation, completed change
to give up, leave alone (= 舍)

exercise.en: How far I have declined! For a long time now I have not dreamed of the Duke of Zhou.
exercise.tests: 矣, 也, 復 (→ L1)
exercise.h_s: 甚矣吾衰也！久矣吾不复梦见周公。

exercise.h: 天生德於予，桓魋其如予何？
exercise.py: Tiān shēng dé yú yú, Huán Tuí qí rú yú hé?
exercise.en: Heaven gave birth to the virtue in me — what can Huan Tui do to me?
exercise.tests: 予
exercise.h_s: 天生德于予，桓魋其如予何？

exercise.py: Zǐ wèi Yán Yuān yuē: Yòng zhī zé xíng, shě zhī zé cáng, wéi wǒ yǔ ěr yǒu shì fú!
exercise.en: The Master said to Yan Yuan: "When employed, act; when set aside, withdraw — only you and I have this!"

lessons.culture: This passage is the second half of Mencius's famous answer on 浩然之氣 (Mencius 2A:2). His advice: keep working at righteousness, "don't forget it, but don't help it grow" (勿忘，勿助長也). The idiom 揠苗助長 (also 拔苗助長 in modern mainland usage) means to spoil something by being too eager, often said of pushy parents and over-ambitious reforms.

lessons.title: 刻舟求劍
lessons.title_en: Notching the Boat to Find the Sword

source.author: compiled under 呂不韋 Lü Buwei (d. 235 BC)
source.text_from: 《呂氏春秋·慎大覽·察今》; first sentence as quoted in 王力《古代漢語》 (with 於 for its 于), the rest matched against two published editions.

lessons.intro: The *Springs and Autumns of Master Lü* is an encyclopedia commissioned by Lü Buwei, chancellor of Qin, from the scholars he kept at his court. The chapter "Examining the Present" (察今) argues the same point as L1: laws must change with the times. This fable brings two important new tools: 所, which turns a verb into "the place / thing that …", and the rhetorical question 不亦…乎.

lines.py: Chǔ rén yǒu shè jiāng zhě,
lines.en: A man of Chu was crossing the river.
lines.lit: Chu people there-was crossing river one

lines.py: qí jiàn zì zhōu zhōng zhuì yú shuǐ,
lines.en: His sword fell from the boat into the water.
At once he cut a notch in the boat, saying:

lines.py: Shì wú jiàn zhī suǒ cóng zhuì.
lines.en: "This is where my sword fell from."
When the boat stopped,

lines.py: cóng qí suǒ qì zhě rù shuǐ qiú zhī.
lines.en: he went into the water from the place he had notched, to look for it.
The boat had moved on,
but the sword had not.
To look for a sword like this —
isn't that foolish?

lines.py: Yǐ cǐ gù fǎ wéi qí guó,
lines.en: To run one's state with these old laws
is just the same.
The times have moved on,
but the laws have not;
to govern like this —
how could it not be hard!

notes.text: **涉** shè "to cross (a river), wade". **江** jiāng is *the* River, the Yangzi, just as 河 is the Yellow River. Only later did 江 and 河 become general words for "river" (古今詞義). 楚人有涉江者 has the same shape as L1's opening (→ L1 n.2).

Two prepositions: **自** "from" (自舟中 "from inside the boat") and **於** "into, at" (墜於水 "fell into the water"). Notice the order: 自 phrases come *before* the verb, 於 phrases *after* it. 墜 zhuì "to fall, drop".
**遽** jù "at once, hastily" (modern 立刻 or 急忙); it shows the man's panic. **契** qì "to carve, notch" (the same word is written 鍥). The modern meaning "contract" comes from notched wooden tallies.
**是 = "this"**, not "is" (→ L1 n.11). 是吾劍之所從墜 is a judgment sentence with no verb: "this [is] the place my sword fell from".

**所 + (preposition) + verb = "the place / thing that …"**. 所 makes a verb into a noun phrase that refers to its object or circumstance: 所墜 "what fell"; 所從墜 "where (something) fell *from*". Put a subject + 之 in front: 吾劍之所從墜 "the place my sword fell from". In line 6, 其所契者 "the place he had notched" adds 者 at the end, with no change of meaning.

**已 … 矣** "already … (now)": 已 yǐ "already" before the verb, 矣 (→ L3 n.5) at the end for the completed change. Two different characters both read yǐ. And **行** here is "to move, go", not "to walk" — it's used of the boat (→ L1 n.3).
**若此** "like this" (若 = 如 "to be like"; 此 "this"). 此 is the ordinary demonstrative "this"; 是 (n. 4) is "this" used to sum up or point back.

**不亦 … 乎** is a rhetorical question expecting "yes": "isn't it (also) …?". You already met it in the first line of the 論語 (→ L1 exercise 2: 不亦說乎). **乎** hū is the question particle; **惑** huò "confused, deluded, foolish".

**故** gù here = "old, former" (故法 "old laws"; compare 故鄉 "old home"). **為** wéi "to manage, run": 為國 "to run a state". 以 A 為 B would be "regard A as B", but here 以此故法 is simply "with these old laws" (→ L1 n.10).
**徙** xǐ "to move, shift" — used of people, capitals, and here of the times. The author mirrors the story: the boat moved, the sword didn't; the times moved, the laws didn't.
**豈 … 哉** "how could …?!": 豈 qǐ starts a rhetorical question, 哉 zāi ends an exclamation. 豈不難哉 "how could it not be difficult!" = it is certainly difficult.

exercise.h: 學而時習之，不亦說乎？有朋自遠方來，不亦樂乎？
exercise.py: Xué ér shí xí zhī, bù yì yuè hū? Yǒu péng zì yuǎn fāng lái, bù yì lè hū?
exercise.en: To learn and practise it at the right times — is that not a pleasure? To have friends come from afar — is that not a joy?
exercise.tests: 不亦…乎, 自
exercise.h_s: 学而时习之，不亦说乎？有朋自远方来，不亦乐乎？

exercise.h: 己所不欲，勿施於人。
exercise.py: Jǐ suǒ bù yù, wù shī yú rén.
exercise.en: What you yourself do not want, do not do to others.
exercise.tests: 所 (所不欲 "what one doesn't want"), 於
exercise.h_s: 己所不欲，勿施于人。

exercise.h: 是可忍也，孰不可忍也？
exercise.py: Shì kě rěn yě, shú bù kě rěn yě?
exercise.en: If this can be tolerated, what cannot?
exercise.tests: 是 = this, 可 + verb (→ L1 n.8)
exercise.h_s: 是可忍也，孰不可忍也？

exercise.h: 逝者如斯夫！不舍晝夜。
exercise.py: Shì zhě rú sī fú! Bù shě zhòu yè.
exercise.en: What passes away is like this, day and night without ceasing!
exercise.tests: 如 = 若, 者, 夫 (exclamatory, at the end)
exercise.h_s: 逝者如斯夫！不舍昼夜。

lessons.culture: Lü Buwei, a merchant, became chancellor of Qin and patron of the young king who would become the First Emperor. He had the book displayed at the gate of the Qin capital and offered a thousand pieces of gold to anyone who could add or remove a single character (一字千金). Like Han Fei, the authors of 察今 argue against copying the laws of the ancient kings: "times change, so laws must change".

lessons.title: 畫蛇添足

source.author: anonymous; compiled by 劉向 Liu Xiang (77–6 BC)
source.text_from: 《戰國策·齊策二·昭陽為楚伐魏》, the standard text, matched against a published edition and the 古汉语常用字字典's quotation of the last line; punctuation modernised.

lessons.intro: The *Intrigues of the Warring States* collects the speeches of travelling persuaders, men who went from court to court selling strategies. Here the persuader 陳軫 Chen Zhen meets a Chu general who has just won a great victory and wants to attack the state of Qi as well. He tells him this story to say: you already have the wine — stop while you're ahead. New in this lesson: the "not yet" negative 未, the question word 安 "how", and 為 meaning "to make".

lines.en: In Chu there was a man who made a sacrifice to his ancestors.

lines.py: cì qí shè rén zhī jiǔ.
lines.en: He gave his retainers a flagon of wine.
The retainers said to one another:

lines.py: Shù rén yǐn zhī bù zú,
lines.en: "For several of us to drink it, it's not enough;

lines.py: yī rén yǐn zhī yǒu yú.
lines.en: for one to drink it, there's more than enough.
Let's each draw a snake on the ground,
and whoever finishes first drinks the wine."
One man's snake was done first.
He pulled the wine towards him and was about to drink it,
but then, holding the flagon in his left hand,
and drawing on the snake with his right, he said:
"I can give it feet!"
Before he had finished,
another man's snake was done.
He snatched the flagon and said:
"Snakes have no feet, of course:

lines.py: zǐ ān néng wéi zhī zú?
lines.en: how can you give it feet?"
And so he drank the wine.
The one who drew feet on the snake
lost his wine in the end.

notes.text: **祠** cí "to make an offering (to ancestors or spirits)". After the rite the sacrificial wine was shared out. 楚有祠者 "in Chu there was one who sacrificed": the 有…者 opening again (→ L1 n.2), this time with a place (楚) as the topic.

**舍人** shè rén "retainers, household men" (舍 "lodging": those who lodged in his house). **卮** zhī is a wine flagon; 卮酒 "a flagon of wine" — the container works as a measure word. **賜** cì "to give (from a superior)". 賜 + person + thing: two objects, as in English "gave his men wine".
**相** xiāng before a verb = "each other, mutually": 相謂 "said to each other". (It can also mean "to someone", as in modern 相信, but here it's reciprocal.)

**數** shù "several" (read shǔ as the verb "to count"). The two lines are a perfect parallel pair: 數人飲之 | 不足 / 一人飲之 | 有餘. **足** "enough" and **餘** "surplus". The whole story will pun on 足, which also means "foot".
**請** qǐng "please (let us) …": a polite proposal. **畫地為蛇** "draw on the ground to make a snake": 為 wéi "to make, to be (as)".
**且** qiě before a verb = "about to": 且飲之 "was about to drink it". (Elsewhere 且 means "and, moreover".) **引** yǐn "to draw, pull towards oneself".
**乃** nǎi "then, thereupon", often with a sense of surprise or contrast: "but then he …". Compare 因 (→ L1 n.5) and 遂 (n. 11).

**為之足** wéi zhī zú "make feet for it": 為 takes two objects, 之 "it (the snake)" and 足 "feet". Some editions and teachers read it wèi zhī zú "draw feet *for* it", with 為 as a preposition; the meaning is the same.
**未** wèi = "not yet". 未成 "(he had) not yet finished". Compare 不 (simple "not") and 弗 (→ L2 n.8). 未 often implies "but it will / should happen".
**固** gù "certainly, by nature, of course": 蛇固無足 "snakes, by their nature, have no feet". **安** ān in line 17 is a question word, "how? where?": 子安能 "how can you …?" — not "peaceful".
**遂** suì "and so, thereupon, then (as a result)". **飲其酒** "drank *his* wine": 其 is the would-be winner's — it was his by rights.

**亡** wáng = "to lose" (and "to flee, to perish"), not only "to die". 終亡其酒 "in the end lost his wine". **終** zhōng "in the end". The idiom 畫蛇添足 "draw a snake and add feet" means to spoil something by overdoing it.

exercise.h: 未知生，焉知死？
exercise.py: Wèi zhī shēng, yān zhī sǐ?
exercise.en: Not yet understanding life, how could one understand death?
exercise.tests: 未, 焉 = 安 "how"
exercise.h_s: 未知生，焉知死？

exercise.h: 亡羊而補牢，未為遲也。
exercise.py: Wáng yáng ér bǔ láo, wèi wéi chí yě.
exercise.en: To mend the pen after losing a sheep is not yet too late.
exercise.tests: 亡 = lose, 未, 而
exercise.h_s: 亡羊而补牢，未为迟也。

exercise.h: 泉涸，魚相與處於陸，相呴以濕，相濡以沫，不如相忘於江湖。
exercise.py: Quán hé, yú xiāng yǔ chǔ yú lù, xiāng xǔ yǐ shī, xiāng rú yǐ mò, bù rú xiāng wàng yú jiāng hú.
exercise.en: When the spring dries up, the fish are left together on dry land; they moisten each other with their breath and wet each other with their spittle. Better to forget each other in the rivers and lakes.
exercise.tests: 相 = each other, 於
exercise.h_s: 泉涸，鱼相与处于陆，相呴以湿，相濡以沫，不如相忘于江湖。

lessons.culture: The frame story: 昭陽 Zhao Yang, chief minister and general of Chu, has crushed Wei and is marching on Qi. Qi sends 陳軫 Chen Zhen to him. After the fable Chen Zhen points out that Zhao Yang already holds the highest rank Chu can give; even if he wins, he gains nothing more, and if he loses, he loses everything — like the man who drew the feet. Zhao Yang turned back.

lessons.title: 狐假虎威
lessons.title_en: The Fox Borrows the Tiger's Might

source.author: anonymous; compiled by 劉向 Liu Xiang (77–6 BC)
source.text_from: 《戰國策·楚策一·江乙對荊宣王》, as printed in 王力《古代漢語》 unit 1; its dash before 猶 is replaced by a comma.

lessons.intro: The first fable told *inside* a conversation, the way persuaders actually used them. King Xuan of Chu (here called 荊, an old name for Chu) asks why the northern states fear his minister Zhao Xixu. Jiang Yi, a rival of Zhao's, answers with a story. Watch three things: the 之 of L2 doing heavy work in long sentences, 以 A 為 B "to regard A as B", and two words, 地方 and 其實, that look modern but aren't.

lines.py: Jīng Xuān wáng wèn qún chén yuē:
lines.en: King Xuan of Jing asked his ministers:

lines.py: Wú wén běi fāng zhī wèi Zhāo Xīxù yě,
lines.en: "I hear that the north fears Zhao Xixu.
Is it really so?"
None of the ministers answered.
Jiang Yi replied:

lines.py: Hǔ qiú bǎi shòu ér shí zhī,
lines.en: "A tiger was hunting all the beasts to eat them,
and caught a fox.

lines.py: Hú yuē: Zǐ wú gǎn shí wǒ yě!
lines.en: The fox said: 'Don't you dare eat me!

lines.py: Tiān dì shǐ wǒ zhǎng bǎi shòu,
lines.en: The Lord of Heaven has made me chief of all the beasts;
if you eat me now,

lines.py: shì nì tiān dì mìng yě.
lines.en: that is defying the Lord of Heaven's command.

lines.py: Zǐ yǐ wǒ wéi bù xìn,
lines.en: If you think I'm lying,
lines.lit: you take me as not truthful

lines.en: I'll walk ahead of you,
you follow behind me,

lines.h: 觀百獸之見我而敢不走乎？』
lines.py: guān bǎi shòu zhī jiàn wǒ ér gǎn bù zǒu hū?
lines.en: and see whether a single beast that sees me dares not run!'
lines.h_s: 观百兽之见我而敢不走乎？』

lines.en: The tiger thought he was right,
so it went along with him.
The beasts saw them and all ran.

lines.py: Hǔ bù zhī shòu wèi jǐ ér zǒu yě,
lines.en: The tiger didn't realise the beasts ran because they feared *it*;
it thought they feared the fox.

lines.py: Jīn wáng zhī dì fāng wǔ qiān lǐ,
lines.en: Now Your Majesty's land is five thousand li on each side,
with a million men in armour,

lines.py: ér zhuān zhǔ zhī Zhāo Xīxù.
lines.en: and you have entrusted them all to Zhao Xixu.

lines.py: Gù běi fāng zhī wèi Xīxù yě,
lines.en: So when the north fears Xixu,

lines.py: qí shí wèi wáng zhī jiǎ bīng yě,
lines.en: what it really fears is Your Majesty's army,

lines.py: yóu bǎi shòu zhī wèi hǔ yě.
lines.en: just as the beasts feared the tiger."

notes.text: **荊** Jīng is another name for Chu (楚). 宣王 King Xuan reigned 369–340 BC. **群臣** "the assembled ministers". The 戰國策 is full of scenes like this: a king asks, the court falls silent, one adviser speaks.

**Subject + 之 + predicate as an object** (→ L2 n.3). 北方畏昭奚恤 would be a sentence, "the north fears Zhao Xixu"; with 之 it becomes a noun phrase, "the north's fearing Zhao Xixu", the object of 聞 "I hear (of)". The final 也 marks a pause before the question. The same pattern returns in lines 15, 24 and 26.
**果** and **誠** both mean "really, truly" (果 survives in 果然 "sure enough"). 何如 "how is it?" (→ L2 n.7).
**莫** "no one" (→ L2 n.4). **對** duì = to reply *to a superior*: ministers 對 the king; the king 問 or 曰.
**食** shí "to eat" (the modern word is 吃). Read sì when it means "to feed someone". 求 here is "to hunt for, look for" (→ L4).
**無** here = **毋** wú "don't!": a prohibition. 子無敢食我也 "don't you dare eat me". Classical Chinese uses 無/毋 and 勿 for "don't", where modern Chinese says 別 or 不要.
**使 A V** "make A do V, have A V": a causative. **長** zhǎng (→ L3 n.2) "chief" used as a verb: 長百獸 "to be chief of the hundred beasts". 百獸 "the hundred beasts" = all animals.
**是** = "this (that you'd be doing)" (→ L4 n.4). 是逆天帝命也 "this is defying the Lord of Heaven's command" — 也 closes the judgment (→ L1 n.11). **逆** nì "to go against, defy".

**以 A 為 B** "to regard A as B": 以我為不信 "regard me as untruthful". Two lines later, 以為 (→ L3 n.10) "to think" is the same structure with the A left out: 虎以為然 "the tiger considered (it) right". **信** xìn "truthful, trustworthy"; **然** rán "so, right".

**為** wèi "for, on behalf of": 為子先行 "walk ahead for you". Contrast 為 wéi "to be, to make" (L4, L5). And **行** = "walk" vs **走** = "run" (line 15): both in the same breath, the clearest proof of → L1 n.3.
**敢不 V 乎** "dare not V?": a rhetorical question meaning "none will dare *not* run" = they will all run. **觀** guān "to observe, watch".
**己** jǐ "oneself": 畏己 "feared *it* (the tiger itself)". 己 refers back to the subject of the main clause, 虎.

**地方 is two words!** Read 地 | 方五千里: "(your) land — five thousand li square", i.e. five thousand li from east to west and from north to south. Modern 地方 "place" is a later compound; reading it here would be a classic 古今 mistake. (A 里 lǐ was roughly 400 m.)
**帶甲** "wearing armour" = armoured soldiers. **屬** zhǔ (line 23) "to entrust": 專屬之昭奚恤 "entrust them solely to Zhao Xixu", with 之 = "them" (the million soldiers) and 昭奚恤 as the second object.

**其實** = "the reality of it", not the modern adverb "actually". The sentence is: [北方之畏 奚恤也] subject, [其實] "its reality", [畏王之甲兵也] predicate: "the north's fearing Xixu — the truth of it is fearing Your Majesty's armies". 甲兵 "armour and weapons" = the army.
**猶** yóu "to be like, just as" (also "still"). Jiang Yi closes by mapping the fable onto the court: king = tiger, Zhao Xixu = fox. That's the persuader's art: never say it directly.

exercise.h: 知之為知之，不知為不知，是知也。
exercise.py: Zhī zhī wéi zhī zhī, bù zhī wéi bù zhī, shì zhī yě.
exercise.en: To count what you know as knowing it, and what you don't know as not knowing it — that is knowledge.
exercise.tests: 為 = count as, 是 = this, 也
exercise.h_s: 知之为知之，不知为不知，是知也。

exercise.h: 人而無信，不知其可也。
exercise.py: Rén ér wú xìn, bù zhī qí kě yě.
exercise.en: A person without trustworthiness — I don't know how that could work.
exercise.tests: 信, 無, 其
exercise.h_s: 人而无信，不知其可也。

exercise.h: 過猶不及。
exercise.py: Guò yóu bù jí.
exercise.en: Going too far is just like falling short.
exercise.tests: 猶
exercise.h_s: 过犹不及。

lessons.culture: The fox's trick gave Chinese the idiom 狐假虎威 "the fox borrows the tiger's majesty" (假 jiǎ "to borrow" — the word itself is not in the story). It is used of underlings who throw their weight around on the strength of a powerful patron. Jiang Yi's real target was his rival Zhao Xixu: by reminding the king whose power it really was, he cut Zhao down to size.

lessons.title: 複習一
lessons.intro: Six fables, about 300 characters, and most of the machinery of Classical Chinese prose is already in place. Re-read the six texts once more, aloud, with Cover on. Then go through the points below: each one sends you back to the note where it was first explained. Finish with the exercise: six new sentences from the 論語, using only what you've met.

recap.topic: 有 … 者: bringing a character on stage
recap.text: Place or group + 有 + verb phrase + 者 = "there was one (from X) who …". Every fable but L6 opens this way: 宋人有耕者 · 楚人有鬻楯與矛者 · 宋人有閔其苗之不長而揠之者 · 楚人有涉江者 · 楚有祠者.

(1) between two nouns, like 的: 先王之政. (2) after a verb, "him / it / them": 譽之, 求之. (3) between subject and predicate, turning a sentence into a noun phrase: 吾楯之堅 "the hardness of my shield", 北方之畏昭奚恤 "the north's fearing Zhao Xixu". (4) as a verb, "to go to" — not seen yet, but coming.
也 closes a statement of what *is*: 皆守株之類也, A者 B者也. 矣 marks what *has come to be*: 今日病矣, 苗則槁矣, 舟已行矣. A sentence with no verb + 也 is the Classical "A is B"; 是 still means "this".

不 plain "not" · 弗 "not (it)" · 未 "not yet" · 非 "it is not that" · 無/毋 "there is no; don't!" — plus 莫 "no one / nothing", a pronoun with the negation built in. Double negatives make strong positives: 無不陷 "pierces everything".
者 follows a verb phrase: "one who V's" (耕者, 先成者, 為蛇足者). 所 precedes a verb: "what / where one V's" (所從墜 "where it fell from", 所契 "what he'd notched").

recap.topic: Words that changed meaning (古今詞義)
recap.text: 走 run (not walk) · 行 walk / move · 趨 hurry · 病 exhausted · 江 the Yangzi · 亡 lose · 身 oneself · 地方 "land … square" · 其實 "the reality of it".
不亦…乎 "isn't it …?" · 豈…哉 "how could …!" · 安 "how?" · 敢不…乎 "would dare not …?". All of them expect the listener to agree.
以 X V "use X to V" · 以 A 為 B "regard A as B" · 以為 "think that". 為 wéi "to be, make, run" · 為 wèi "for" · 為 A V "be V'ed by A" (passive).

exercise.h: 三人行，必有我師焉。
exercise.py: Sān rén xíng, bì yǒu wǒ shī yān.
exercise.en: When three people walk together, there is sure to be a teacher for me among them.
exercise.tests: 行 = walk, 有
exercise.h_s: 三人行，必有我师焉。

exercise.h: 朝聞道，夕死可矣。
exercise.py: Zhāo wén dào, xī sǐ kě yǐ.
exercise.en: Hear the Way in the morning, and one may die in the evening.
exercise.tests: 聞, 可, 矣
exercise.h_s: 朝闻道，夕死可矣。

exercise.h: 吾日三省吾身：為人謀而不忠乎？與朋友交而不信乎？傳不習乎？
exercise.py: Wú rì sān xǐng wú shēn: wèi rén móu ér bù zhōng hū? Yǔ péngyǒu jiāo ér bù xìn hū? Chuán bù xí hū?
exercise.en: Every day I examine myself on three points: in planning for others, have I been less than loyal? With friends, have I been less than trustworthy? Have I passed on what I have not practised?
exercise.tests: 吾, 身, 為 wèi, 而, 與, 信, 乎
exercise.h_s: 吾日三省吾身：为人谋而不忠乎？与朋友交而不信乎？传不习乎？

exercise.h: 歲寒，然後知松柏之後凋也。
exercise.py: Suì hán, rán hòu zhī sōng bǎi zhī hòu diāo yě.
exercise.en: Only when the year turns cold do we know that pines and cypresses are the last to wither.
exercise.tests: 之 between subject and predicate, 也
exercise.h_s: 岁寒，然后知松柏之后凋也。

exercise.h: 其身正，不令而行；其身不正，雖令不從。
exercise.py: Qí shēn zhèng, bù lìng ér xíng; qí shēn bù zhèng, suī lìng bù cóng.
exercise.en: If he himself is upright, things get done without orders; if he himself is not upright, even his orders are not followed.
exercise.tests: 其, 身, 而, 從
exercise.h_s: 其身正，不令而行；其身不正，虽令不从。

exercise.h: 工欲善其事，必先利其器。
exercise.py: Gōng yù shàn qí shì, bì xiān lì qí qì.
exercise.en: A craftsman who wants to do his work well must first sharpen his tools.
exercise.tests: 欲, 先, 利 (as a verb), 其
exercise.h_s: 工欲善其事，必先利其器。

lessons.title: 濫竽充數
lessons.title_en: Padding Out the Band with a Fake Yu Player

source.author: 韓非 (c. 280–233 BC)
source.text_from: 《韓非子·內儲說上七術》. Lines 1–9 as quoted on English Wiktionary 濫竽充數 (CC BY-SA), with the comma after 吹竽 that Wiktionary leaves out; lines 10–15 (the 一曰 version) typed from the unpunctuated 四庫全書 文淵閣 text (Kanseki Repository KR3c0005, 卷九), punctuation ours. Compared line by line, 2026-11-19, with that 文淵閣 text and with the 殆知閣 transcription; the three agree word for word (文淵閣 writes the variant forms 廪 and 聴 for 廩 and 聽).

lessons.intro: Back to Han Fei. The "Inner Collection of Sayings" (內儲說) is a teaching anthology: Han Fei states a principle of rule, then piles up anecdotes as evidence. This one illustrates "hear each man separately" (一聽): a ruler who only listens to his officials in a crowd can't tell the good from the useless. Watch for 說 read yuè (a character standing for another word), the reading 好 hào, and the very common 無以 "have no way to".

lines.py: Qí Xuān wáng shǐ rén chuī yú,
lines.en: When King Xuan of Qi had the yu played,
it had to be by three hundred men at once.

lines.py: Nánguō chǔ shì qǐng wèi wáng chuī yú,
lines.en: A gentleman of leisure from the Southern Wall asked to play the yu for the king.
King Xuan was pleased with him,

lines.py: lǐn sì yǐ shù bǎi rén.
lines.en: and fed him from the state granary along with those several hundred men.
King Xuan died
and King Min came to the throne.
He liked to hear them one by one,
and the gentleman ran away.
Another version says:
Marquis Zhao of Han said:
"There are many yu players;

lines.py: wú wú yǐ zhī qí shàn zhě.
lines.en: I have no way of knowing which of them are good."
lines.lit: I have-nothing-with-which to-know their good ones

lines.en: Tian Yan answered:
"Listen to them one at a time."

notes.text: **齊宣王** King Xuan of Qi (reigned 319–301 BC), the king Mencius talks to in the 孟子. 使人吹竽 "had people play the yu": the causative 使 A V (→ L6 n.7). **竽** yú is a large mouth organ, a gourd wind-chest with bamboo pipes, the bass of the 笙 family; it was played in big court ensembles.

**A noun phrase as the predicate.** 必三百人 has no verb: "(it) necessarily (was) three hundred men". Classical Chinese can make a number or a noun phrase the comment on a topic, with an adverb (必 bì "necessarily, without fail") in front of it. This is the judgment sentence of → L1 n.11 without its 也, and it is common with numbers: 年且九十 "his age (was) nearly ninety" will come in L12.

**處士** chǔ shì, not "a person who handles things". 處 chǔ is "to dwell, stay at home"; a 處士 is a man of education who *stays home*, holding no office. That's the joke: a gentleman of leisure joins the palace band, with a salary. (處 chù "place" is the noun.) **南郭** Nánguō "Southern Outer Wall" (郭 the outer city wall) is where he lived, used as his name; in the idiom he is 南郭先生, "Mr Nanguo".

**請 + verb = "ask to (be allowed to)"**: 請為王吹竽 "asked to play the yu for the king". The one who asks is the one who will act. In L5, 請畫地為蛇 was a proposal to the group, "let's draw" (→ L5 n.5): same word, said to equals. 為 wèi "for" (→ L6 n.10).

**說 = 悅 yuè "to be pleased (with)".** Ancient scribes often wrote a word with the character of another word that sounded the same or close: the "borrowed character" (通假字). The reading follows the word meant, not the character: 說 here is yuè, not shuō. 悅 is a later character made for this word, and many texts use it; the 論語 keeps 說 (不亦說乎, → L1 exercise 2). 說 has three readings in this course: shuō "to say, explain", shuì "to persuade (a ruler)", yuè "pleased". 宣王說之 "King Xuan was pleased with him": 之 is the object (→ L2 n.2).

**廩** lǐn "public granary". Put before the verb, the noun says *how* or *from where* the action is done: 廩食 "feed from the granary". **食** is sì "to feed" (→ L6 n.5). 以數百人 is the hard part: commentators read it "on the same footing as the several hundred men" (the sense of our translation) or "with rations for several hundred men". Either way, the impostor was on the state payroll. (Nouns used as adverbs come back in L10.)

**立** lì "to stand" (→ L2 n.10), said of a ruler: "to be set up, to come to the throne". 宣王死， 湣王立 is the formula of every chronicle: "X died and Y succeeded". King Min (reigned 300–284 BC) was Xuan's son.

**好** has two readings (破音字, → L3 n.2): hǎo "good" and **hào "to like, be fond of"**, the verb here. **一一** yī yī "one by one": a doubled numeral used as an adverb. 聽之 "listen to them" (之 → L2 n.2). The new king's taste for solos is the end of the impostor.

**一曰** "one (account) says": Han Fei tells the story again in another version, the way the 儲說 chapters often do. In this one the ruler is **韓昭侯** Marquis Zhao of Han (reigned 362–333 BC; 侯 hóu "marquis", a lower rank than 王), who employed the statesman 申不害.
**眾** zhòng "many, numerous", the opposite of 寡 (→ L3 n.9). The subject is a 者 phrase (→ L1 n.2): 吹竽者 "those who play the yu".

**無以 V = "to have nothing with which to V", i.e. "have no way to, be unable to".** Read it as 無 (→ L2 n.5) + 以 "by means of (it)" (→ L1 n.10) with the "it" left out. Its opposite is 有以 V "have the means to V". 無以 is one of the commonest phrases in prose; expect it again in L13 (written 亡以, with 亡 for 無).
**其 + adjective + 者** = "those of them who are …": 其善者 "the good ones among them". 其 "their" (→ L1 n.6) marks the group, 者 (→ L1 n.2) picks out the members.

Tian Yan's answer puts 而 between the manner and the verb: 一一**而**聽之 "one by one, listen to them" (→ L2 n.10). It is the same advice as King Min's taste for solos: test officials one at a time, and the impostors will run.

glossary.en: Qi, a great state of the east (in present-day Shandong)
to blow; to play (a wind instrument)
the Southern Outer Wall (used as a name)
a gentleman out of office, a scholar living at home
Han, a central state (in present-day Henan and Shanxi)
marquis, ruler of a state below the rank of king
to have no way to, be unable to

exercise.h: 近者說，遠者來。
exercise.py: Jìn zhě yuè, yuǎn zhě lái.
exercise.en: (Govern so that) those near are pleased and those far away come.
exercise.tests: 說 = 悅 yuè, 者
exercise.h_s: 近者说，远者来。

exercise.h: 知之者不如好之者，好之者不如樂之者。
exercise.py: Zhī zhī zhě bù rú hào zhī zhě, hào zhī zhě bù rú lè zhī zhě.
exercise.en: Those who know it are not as good as those who love it; those who love it are not as good as those who delight in it.
exercise.tests: 好 hào, 者
exercise.h_s: 知之者不如好之者，好之者不如乐之者。

exercise.h: 不知命，無以為君子也；不知禮，無以立也；不知言，無以知人也。
exercise.py: Bù zhī mìng, wú yǐ wéi jūnzǐ yě; bù zhī lǐ, wú yǐ lì yě; bù zhī yán, wú yǐ zhī rén yě.
exercise.en: Without understanding fate, one has no way to be a gentleman; without understanding the rites, no way to take one's stand; without understanding words, no way to understand people.
exercise.tests: 無以 ×3, 立
exercise.h_s: 不知命，无以为君子也；不知礼，无以立也；不知言，无以知人也。

exercise.h: 王說曰：「詩云：『他人有心，予忖度之。』夫子之謂也。」
exercise.py: Wáng yuè yuē: Shī yún: Tā rén yǒu xīn, yú cǔn duó zhī. Fūzǐ zhī wèi yě.
exercise.en: The king was pleased and said: "The Songs say: 'Another man has a heart; I guess at it and measure it.' That is what you have done, Master."
exercise.tests: 說 = 悅 yuè, 予 (→ L3 n.6); 齊宣王 again, talking to Mencius
exercise.h_s: 王说曰：「诗云：『他人有心，予忖度之。』夫子之谓也。」

lessons.culture: The idiom 濫竽充數 "an unqualified yu (player) filling up the numbers" (濫 "excessive, unworthy") is said of anyone who holds a place without the skill for it, and very often of oneself, out of modesty: 我只是濫竽充數 "I'm only here to make up the numbers". Han Fei's point was harder: a ruler who never tests his officials one by one will feed hundreds of impostors.

lessons.title: 鄭人買履
lessons.title_en: The Man of Zheng Buys Shoes

source.author: 韓非 (c. 280–233 BC)
source.text_from: 《韓非子·外儲說左上》, as printed in the Hong Kong EDB recommended classical passages (KS2-03). Compared line by line, 2026-11-19, with the English Wiktionary quotation (鄭人買履, CC BY-SA) and the unpunctuated 四庫全書 文淵閣 text (Kanseki Repository KR3c0005, 卷十一): same words throughout. Wiktionary puts 反歸取之 inside the quotation; the idiom's 買 is not in the text (see n. 2).

lessons.intro: The "Outer Collection of Sayings" (外儲說) works like the inner one (L8): principle first, then stories. This one comes in a section about scholars who trust their books more than the facts in front of them. The fool this time is from Zheng. Watch the small words: 之 used as a *verb*, 自 "oneself" placed before its verb, and 度 read two ways.

lines.py: Zhèng rén yǒu qiě zhì lǚ zhě,
lines.en: A man of Zheng was about to buy some shoes.
lines.lit: Zheng people there-was about-to acquire shoes one

lines.h: 先自度其足而置之其坐。
lines.py: xiān zì duó qí zú ér zhì zhī qí zuò.
lines.en: First he measured his feet himself and put (the measurement) on his seat.
lines.h_s: 先自度其足而置之其坐。

lines.en: When it came to going to the market,
he forgot to take it with him.
He had already found the shoes
when he said:
"I forgot to bring the measurement."
He went back home to fetch it.
By the time he came back,
the market had closed,
and so he never got his shoes.
Someone said:

lines.py: Hé bù shì zhī yǐ zú?
lines.en: "Why didn't you try them on with your feet?"
lines.lit: why not try them with feet

lines.en: He said:
"I'd rather trust the measurement
than trust myself."

notes.text: **鄭** Zhèng, a small state in present-day central Henan, swallowed by Han in 375 BC. Like Song (→ L1 n.1), it supplies fools to the philosophers. The opening is the 有 … 者 frame of → L1 n.2.

**置** zhì "to acquire, buy" here; in the next line, 置之其坐, the same word is "to put, place", its everyday sense. **且** "about to" (→ L5 n.6). **履** lǚ "shoe" (in modern Chinese 履 survives in 履行 "to carry out", lit. "to tread"). Many modern school editions rewrite the line as 鄭人有欲買履者, with the commoner words 欲 and 買, and the idiom became 鄭人買履; the transmitted text has 且置.

**自 = "oneself", and it always comes *before* the verb.** 自度其足 "measured his feet himself": here 自 says who does it. In line 16, 自信 "trust oneself", 自 is the *object*, and it still stands before the verb (English says "trust myself"; Classical Chinese says "self-trust"). Modern 自信 "self-confident" grew out of this phrase. Don't confuse it with 自 "from" (→ L4 n.2), which governs a place: 自舟中.

**度** has two readings (破音字, → L3 n.2): **duó** "to measure" (the verb, here) and **dù** "a measure, the measurement" (the noun, in lines 7 and 15). In this story the measurement is a piece of string or a notched stick, something you can put on a chair and forget at home.

置之其坐 "put it on his seat": 之 "it" (the measurement, → L2 n.2), then the place 其坐 with no preposition: the full form would be 置之**於**其坐 (→ L4 n.2). **坐** zuò is the noun "seat" here; the character 座 was made for that sense later (a 古今字, see n. 9).

**之 as a verb: "to go to".** This is the fourth use of 之 promised in Review 1: 之市 "go to the market". 至 "to reach, come to": 至之市 "when (the time) came to go to the market". Some teachers read 至 "arrived" and 之 "at the market"; the verb reading is the standard one. Every 之 so far: attributive (→ L1 n.10), object "it" (→ L2 n.2), between subject and predicate (→ L2 n.3), and now "to go".

**操** cāo "to hold in the hand, carry" (the hand radical 扌 shows it). Modern 操 means "to drill, exercise" (體操) or "to operate" (操作), far from its root. 而 here turns the story: "and yet he forgot" (→ L1 n.9).

**已 … 乃 …** "he had already got the shoes when he (only then) said …": 已 "already" (→ L4 n.6), 乃 "then, thereupon", with the note of surprise of → L5 n.7. 得 here is "to find, get hold of" (the shoes he wanted), not yet "to buy".

**反 = 返 fǎn "to go back".** The old character 反 "to turn over" also wrote "to return"; later a movement radical (辶) was added to make 返 for that sense. A pair like 反/返 or 坐/座 is a **古今字** ("old and new characters"): the *same word*, with a newer spelling. A 通假字 (→ L8 n.5) is different: a character borrowed for an *unrelated* word that sounded alike. Either way, read the word meant.
**及** jí "to reach": before a clause it means "by the time …": 及反 "by the time he got back". **罷** bà "to stop, break up": 市罷 "the market had broken up". 遂 "and so, in the end" (→ L5 n.11).
**何不 V = "why not V?"** 何 asks "what?", and before a verb it asks "why?". Like every question word, it stands before the verb (→ L2 n.7, 何如). A 何不 question is usually advice: "why didn't you just …?"

**V 之以 X = 以 X V 之** "V it with X". The 以 phrase usually comes before the verb (→ L1 n.10), but it may also follow the verb and its object: 試之以足 "try them with your feet" = 以足試之. Both orders are common; after the verb is a little more emphatic about the means.

**寧 A，無 B** "rather A than B": 寧 nìng (not níng "peaceful") "would rather"; 無 is the prohibitive "don't" (→ L6 n.6), here "rather not". 寧信度，無自信 "I'd rather trust the measurement than trust myself", the whole moral in six characters.

**自信** "trust oneself", with 自 as the object before the verb (n. 3). Han Fei's target is the scholar who believes the books of the ancients rather than what he can see: the same quarrel with the "former kings" as in L1.

glossary.en: Zheng, a small central state (in present-day Henan)
to acquire, buy (line 1); to put, place (line 2)
to measure; read dù: a measure, the measurement
to reach; when it came to

exercise.py: Wáng jiàn zhī, yuē: Niú hé zhī?
exercise.en: The king saw it and said: "Where is the ox going?"
exercise.tests: 之 = to go; the question word 何 before the verb
exercise.h_s: 王见之，曰：「牛何之？」

exercise.h: 權，然後知輕重；度，然後知長短。
exercise.py: Quán, rán hòu zhī qīng zhòng; duó, rán hòu zhī cháng duǎn.

exercise.tests: 度 duó, the noun 權 "steelyard" used as the verb "to weigh"
exercise.h_s: 权，然后知轻重；度，然后知长短。

exercise.h: 見賢思齊焉，見不賢而內自省也。
exercise.py: Jiàn xián sī qí yān, jiàn bù xián ér nèi zì xǐng yě.
exercise.en: When you see a worthy man, think of becoming his equal; when you see an unworthy one, look inside and examine yourself.
exercise.tests: 自 + verb (自省 "examine oneself"), 而
exercise.h_s: 见贤思齐焉，见不贤而内自省也。

exercise.h: 禮，與其奢也，寧儉。
exercise.py: Lǐ, yǔ qí shē yě, nìng jiǎn.
exercise.en: In ritual, rather than be lavish, be frugal.
exercise.tests: 寧 nìng "rather"
exercise.h_s: 礼，与其奢也，宁俭。

exercise.h: 殺人以梃與刃，有以異乎？
exercise.py: Shā rén yǐ tǐng yǔ rèn, yǒu yǐ yì hū?
exercise.en: Killing a man with a club or with a blade: is there anything that makes them different?
exercise.tests: 以 phrase after the verb, 有以 (→ L8 n.11), 與, 乎
exercise.h_s: 杀人以梃与刃，有以异乎？

lessons.culture: Han Fei tells the story in a section on scholars who argue from ancient texts instead of from the case in front of them. The idiom 鄭人買履 (also 買履忘度) mocks anyone who sticks to a rule or a document even when the plain facts are at hand: the feet were there all along.

lessons.title: 塞翁失馬
lessons.title_en: The Old Man at the Frontier Loses His Horse

source.author: compiled at the court of 劉安 Liu An, King of Huainan (179–122 BC)
source.text_from: 《淮南子·人間訓》, as quoted on English Wiktionary 塞翁失馬，焉知非福 (CC BY-SA). Compared line by line, 2026-11-19, with the English Wikipedia article "The old man lost his horse" and with the unpunctuated 四庫全書 文淵閣 text (淮南鴻烈解, Kanseki Repository KR3j0010, 卷十八). We write 弔 with Wikipedia's variant note and the 文淵閣 text, where Wiktionary has the popular form 吊. The 文淵閣 text also has 引絃 for 引弦 and, in line 18, 何不遽為福 (see n. 7).

lessons.intro: The *Huainanzi* is a large Han-dynasty compendium written by the scholars of Liu An, King of Huainan, and presented to the young Emperor Wu in 139 BC. The chapter "In the World of Men" (人間訓) collects stories about how luck turns. In this one the same sentence comes back three times, so the story is easy to follow; give your attention to the small words: 何遽 in the questions, 故 in three senses, and an adjective used as a verb (家富良馬), the first example of the "shift of word class" (詞類活用) that runs all through Classical Chinese.

lines.py: Fú huò fú zhī zhuǎn ér xiāng shēng,
lines.en: Now, the way misfortune and good fortune turn into each other and give rise to each other —
its changes are hard to see.

lines.py: Jìn sài shàng zhī rén yǒu shàn shù zhě,
lines.en: Among the people who lived near the frontier there was a man skilled in divination.
lines.lit: near frontier-on 's people there-was good-at arts one

lines.py: mǎ wú gù wáng ér rù Hú.
lines.en: His horse ran off for no reason into the land of the Hu.
Everyone came to condole with him.
The father said:

lines.py: Cǐ hé jù bù wéi fú hū?
lines.en: "Who's to say this won't turn into good fortune?"
lines.lit: this how readily not become fortune ?

lines.en: Some months later,

lines.py: qí mǎ jiāng Hú jùn mǎ ér guī.
lines.en: his horse came back, leading a fine horse of the Hu.
Everyone congratulated him.
The father said:

lines.py: Cǐ hé jù bù néng wéi huò hū?
lines.en: "Who's to say this can't turn into misfortune?"
The household was now rich in fine horses,
and his son loved riding.
He fell and broke his thigh.
Everyone came to condole with him.
The father said:

lines.py: Cǐ hé jù bù wéi fú hū?
lines.en: "Who's to say this won't turn into good fortune?"
A year later
the Hu invaded the frontier in force.

lines.py: dīng zhuàng zhě yǐn xián ér zhàn,
lines.en: The able-bodied men drew their bows and fought;
of the people near the frontier,
nine in ten died.

lines.py: cǐ dú yǐ bǒ zhī gù,
lines.en: This one alone, because of the lameness,
father and son both came through safe.
So the way good fortune becomes misfortune
and misfortune becomes good fortune:
its transformations can't be followed to the end,
its depths can't be fathomed.

notes.text: The opening sentence is the author's thesis, and it also closes the story that comes before it in the chapter. 夫 fú "now" announces a general statement (→ L2 n.9). 禍福之轉而相生 is a whole sentence turned into a noun phrase by 之 (→ L2 n.3): "misfortune and fortune's turning and giving rise to each other" (相 "each other", → L5 n.3). 其變 "its changes" picks it up again.

**塞** has two readings: **sài** "frontier pass, border fortress" (here, and in the idiom 塞翁 "the old man of the frontier") and **sè** "to block" (→ L11, L12). 近塞上之人 "the people living near the frontier" is a long modifier + 之 + noun (→ L1 n.10), and 有 … 者 brings the hero on stage (→ L1 n.2).

**善 = "to be good at"** (古今詞義): before a verb or noun, 善 is a skill, not a virtue: 善術 "good at the arts" (compare 我善養吾浩然之氣, exercise 3). **術** shù "art, technique", here the arts of reading omens and fate (數術). Modern 善 leans to "kind" (善良) and 術 to "technique" (技術); both older senses live on in compounds like 善於 "good at" and 算術 "arithmetic".

**故** gù "cause, reason": 無故 "without cause, for no reason". (In L4 故法 was "old laws": → L4 n.9. The two uses look unrelated, but 故 is "what was there before", hence both "old" and "the cause".) **亡** wáng "to run away, go missing" (→ L5 n.12). **胡** Hú: the horse-riding peoples of the northern steppe.

**弔** diào "to offer condolences, commiserate" — not "to hang". The popular form 吊 (the one Wiktionary's text has, and the simplified form) later took on the sense "to hang, suspend". Its opposite comes in line 10: **賀** hè "to congratulate". The story swings between the two.

**其父** qí fù "his father": the father of that household, i.e. the man skilled in divination himself, who is old and has a grown son (父子 in line 25). Wiktionary and most editions read 父 fù; some teachers read it fǔ "old man", a respectful word for an elder, with the same result: he is the 塞翁, the old man of the idiom.

**何遽 … 乎** "how can one be so quick to say …?" 何 "how" + 遽 jù "hastily, at once" (→ L4 n.3) make a rhetorical question (→ L4 n.8): 此何遽不為福乎 "how can you be sure this won't become good fortune?" = it may well do. **為** wéi "to become" (→ L5 n.5). In the third round (line 18) the 四庫全書 text reads 此何不遽為福乎, with the same meaning.
**居** jū "to stay, remain"; with a stretch of time it means "after … had passed": 居數月 "when a few months had gone by", 居一年 "a year later" (line 19). 數 shù "several" (→ L5 n.4).

**將** jiāng "to lead, bring along" (古今詞義): 其馬將胡駿馬而歸 "his horse came back leading a fine Hu horse". Modern 將 is mostly the future marker "will"; the verb survives in the noun 將 jiàng "general, the one who leads". 駿 jùn "fine, swift (of a horse)".

**Shift of word class (詞類活用).** 富 is an adjective, "rich"; followed by an object, it works as a verb: 富良馬 "be rich in fine horses". Classical Chinese marks no word class on the word itself: the slot decides. A noun before a verb can tell *how* (廩食 "feed from the granary", → L8 n.6), a noun with an object becomes a verb (面山 "face the mountain", L12), and an adjective can mean "make (it) so" (平險 "level the steep", L12) or "treat as so" (老吾老 "treat my elders as elders", exercise 2). 王力 groups them all under 詞類活用. Read for the slot, not the dictionary label.
**好騎** hào qí "loved riding" (好 hào → L8 n.8). **墮** duò "to fall"; **髀** bì "thigh, thigh bone", the son's injury that will save his life. 折 "to break" (→ L1).
**大** as an adverb: "on a large scale, in force". 大入塞 "came through the frontier in force", i.e. a full invasion, not a raid.

**丁壯** dīng zhuàng "men in their prime", those liable for service (丁 is still the word for an adult male in old registers). 引弦 "draw the bowstring" (引 "to pull", → L5 n.6). 而 links the two actions (→ L1 n.4).

**十九 = "nine in ten", not "nineteen".** A number followed by a smaller one often gives a proportion: 十九 "nine out of ten", 十一 "one in ten" (the tithe in Mencius). 死者十九 "of those who died, nine tenths": the topic is the people of line 22, the 者 phrase (→ L1 n.2) picks out the dead, and the number is the predicate (→ L8 n.2).

**以 X 之故 = "because of X".** 以 here is "because of" (new: so far it was "with, by means of", → L1 n.10), and 故 is "reason" (n. 4): 以跛之故 "for the reason of the lameness". **獨** dú "alone, only": 此獨 "this one (household) alone". 跛 bǒ "lame".
**相保** "kept each other safe": father and son both survived, the father because he had no fighting son to lose, the son because he couldn't be called up. 相 "each other" (→ L5 n.3).

**故 at the head of a sentence = "therefore, and so"**: the third 故 of the passage (無故 "for no reason", 之故 "the reason", 故 "therefore"); you met it in L6 too (故遂與之行). Then two subject + 之 + predicate phrases as subjects (→ L2 n.3): 福之為禍 "good fortune's becoming misfortune".

**不可 + verb** in its passive sense (→ L1 n.8): 化不可極 "the transformation cannot be followed to its end", 深不可測 "the depth cannot be measured". 極 jí "extreme point" is used as a verb, "to get to the end of", and 深 "deep" as a noun, "the depth": n. 10 again. The two clauses echo the first sentence: 其變難見也.

glossary.en: the Hu, the nomad peoples of the north
how can one be so quick to say …?

exercise.h: 禍兮福之所倚，福兮禍之所伏。
exercise.py: Huò xī fú zhī suǒ yǐ, fú xī huò zhī suǒ fú.

exercise.tests: 禍, 福, 所 (→ L4 n.5); 兮 xī is a pause particle
exercise.h_s: 祸兮福之所倚，福兮祸之所伏。

exercise.h: 老吾老，以及人之老；幼吾幼，以及人之幼。
exercise.py: Lǎo wú lǎo, yǐ jí rén zhī lǎo; yòu wú yòu, yǐ jí rén zhī yòu.
exercise.en: Treat your own elders as elders and extend it to other people's elders; treat your own young as the young and extend it to other people's young.

exercise.h_s: 老吾老，以及人之老；幼吾幼，以及人之幼。

exercise.h: 我善養吾浩然之氣。
exercise.py: Wǒ shàn yǎng wú hào rán zhī qì.
exercise.en: I am good at nourishing my flood-like qi.
exercise.tests: 善 = be good at, -然 (→ L3 n.3)
exercise.h_s: 我善养吾浩然之气。

exercise.h: 吾所以為此者，以先國家之急而後私讎也。
exercise.py: Wú suǒ yǐ wéi cǐ zhě, yǐ xiān guó jiā zhī jí ér hòu sī chóu yě.
exercise.en: The reason I act like this is that I put the urgent needs of the state first and private feuds last.
exercise.tests: 以 = because; 先 and 後 used as verbs; 所以 … 者 "the reason why"
exercise.h_s: 吾所以为此者，以先国家之急而后私雠也。

lessons.culture: The idiom is usually quoted in full, 塞翁失馬，焉知非福 "the old man at the frontier lost his horse — how could one know it wasn't a blessing?", a later wording: 焉 "how" replaces the story's 何遽. It is the classical form of "every cloud has a silver lining", but the Huainanzi's point is bleaker and more Daoist: fortune and misfortune keep turning into each other, and no one can see where the chain ends.

lessons.title: 杞人憂天
lessons.title_en: The Man of Qi Who Feared the Sky Would Fall

source.author: attributed to 列禦寇 Lie Yukou (Warring States); the text as we have it was edited by 張湛 (4th c. AD)
source.period: compiled by the 4th century AD from older material
source.text_from: 《列子·天瑞》, as quoted on English Wiktionary 杞人憂天 (CC BY-SA), whose readings 亡 wú and 舍 shì we follow. Compared line by line, 2026-11-19, with two unpunctuated transcriptions in the Kanseki Repository: the 四部叢刊 text (KR5c0049) and the 四庫全書 文淵閣 text (KR5c0125). Same words throughout; the old editions write the variant forms 徃 (往) and 舎 (舍), and both have a rare variant glyph in 舍然 or 杞 that the transcriptions could not encode.

lessons.intro: The *Liezi* is a Daoist book in the line of the *Zhuangzi*, full of stories that poke fun at ordinary certainties. This one gave Chinese its word for a groundless worry (杞憂, 杞人憂天). It is almost all dialogue, so it is the place to meet the language of conversation: a second-person pronoun (若 "you"), the particles 耳 "only" and 邪 (a question), the question 奈何 "why?" and its split form 奈 … 何 "what can be done about …?". Note also 亡, read wú here.

lines.en: In the state of Qi there was a man
who worried that heaven and earth would collapse and fall,
leaving him nowhere to put himself,
and who gave up sleeping and eating.

lines.py: Yòu yǒu yōu bǐ zhī suǒ yōu zhě,
lines.en: There was another man, who worried about that man's worrying,
lines.lit: also there-was worrying that-one 's what-worried one

lines.en: so he went to put him right, saying:
"Heaven is nothing but piled-up air;
there is no place without air.
You bend and stretch, breathe out and in,

lines.py: zhōng rì zài tiān zhōng xíng zhǐ,
lines.en: you go about all day inside heaven:

lines.py: nài hé yōu bēng zhuì hū?
lines.en: why worry about it collapsing?"
The man said:
"If heaven really is piled-up air,

lines.py: rì yuè xīng xiù bù dāng zhuì yé?
lines.en: won't the sun, moon and stars fall down?"
The one putting him right said:
"The sun, moon and stars

lines.py: yì jī qì zhōng zhī yǒu guāng yào zhě,
lines.en: are just the parts of that piled-up air that shine;
even if they fell,

lines.py: yì bù néng yǒu suǒ zhòng shāng.
lines.en: they couldn't hit or hurt anything."
The man said:
"And what if the earth gives way?"
The one putting him right said:
"The earth is nothing but piled-up clods,
filling the empty space on all four sides;
there is no place without clods.
You stride and step and stamp about,

lines.py: zhōng rì zài dì shàng xíng zhǐ,
lines.en: you go about all day on the earth:
why worry about it giving way?"

lines.py: Qí rén shì rán dà xǐ,
lines.en: The man was relieved and overjoyed,

lines.py: xiǎo zhī zhě yì shì rán dà xǐ.
lines.en: and the one who had put him right was relieved and overjoyed too.

notes.text: **杞** Qǐ, a tiny state in present-day Henan whose rulers claimed descent from the Xia dynasty. The sentence is the 有 … 者 frame (→ L1 n.2) stretched over four lines: 杞國有人 [憂 … ，… ， 廢寢食] 者 "in Qi there was a man who worried …, … and gave up sleeping and eating". With 人 inside the frame, 有人 … 者 is "there was a person who …".

**亡 = 無, read wú**: "not to have, there is no". This 亡 is the same character as 亡 wáng "to lose, run away" (→ L5 n.12, L10 n.4), used for the word 無, which sounded close. When it means "there is no", read it wú, as Wiktionary does. 亡所寄 = 無所寄 "nothing on which (his body could) lodge": 所 + verb (→ L4 n.5) after 無, "nothing that …, nowhere that …". 身 "his own person" (→ L1 n.9).
**廢** fèi "to abandon, give up", not "waste, useless" as in modern 廢物. 寢 qǐn "to sleep (lying down)", 食 shí "to eat": 廢寢食 "gave up sleep and food", the source of the phrase 廢寢忘食.

**彼** bǐ "that, that one", the far demonstrative (此 "this" is the near one, → L4 n.7). It points at a person as well as a thing, so it often works as "he, they": 彼之所憂 "what *that man* worried about". The phrase is subject + 之 + 所 + verb, as in 吾劍之所從墜 (→ L4 n.5). The second man worries about the first man's worry, and that is the joke of the whole story.

**曉** xiǎo "to make (someone) understand, enlighten": 曉之 "put him right". The adjective "clear, bright" (曉 is also "dawn") is used as a verb meaning "make clear to": the causative kind of word-class shift (→ L10 n.10). Modern 曉得 "to know" uses the plain sense. 因 "and so" (→ L1 n.5), 往 "to go" (→ L3 n.7).

**耳** ěr at the end of a sentence = "only, that's all" (it is a fusion of 而已 "and stop"). 天，積氣耳 "heaven — piled-up air, that's all": a judgment sentence, A，B (→ L1 n.11), with 耳 in place of 也. **積** jī "to pile up, accumulate"; **氣** qì "air, vapour", the stuff of which the Chinese cosmos was thought to be made.
**亡處亡氣** wú chù wú qì "there is no place where there is no air": two negatives make "air is everywhere", like 無不 (→ L2 n.5). **處** chù "place" (compare 處 chǔ "to dwell", → L8 n.3).

**若 = "you".** At the head of a clause, before a verb, 若 is a second-person pronoun: 若屈伸呼吸 "*you* bend and stretch, breathe out and in". So far "you" has been 子, the polite form (→ L2 n.7); 若 is plainer, used to equals and inferiors. Coming next: **汝** (also written **女**) rǔ, the everyday "you" (L12), and 爾 ěr. Don't confuse it with 若 "to be like" (→ L4 n.7): the slot tells you which.
**奈何** nài hé "why? how (can)?": 奈何憂崩墜乎 "why worry about it collapsing?". The question word stands before the verb it questions (→ L9 n.11 何不), and 乎 ends the question (→ L4 n.8).

**果** "really, in fact" (→ L6 n.3). At the head of a clause, the sense slides to "if it really is so": 天果積氣 "if heaven really is piled-up air". Classical Chinese often leaves "if" unsaid; the second clause shows that the first was a condition.

**邪** yé (= 耶) is a question particle, like 乎 (→ L4 n.8) but more often in questions that invite a "yes": 不當墜邪 "shouldn't they fall?" Read yé, not xié "evil". **當** dāng "should, ought to"; **星宿** xīng xiù "the stars and constellations": 宿 is xiù when it means a lunar mansion (sù "to lodge" otherwise).
A long noun phrase: [積氣中] 之 [有光耀] 者 "the ones within the piled-up air that have light". The place (積氣中 "in the piled air") + 之 modifies the 者 phrase (→ L1 n.2, L1 n.10). 亦 "just, likewise (air)".
**只使** zhǐ shǐ "even if, supposing": 只使墜 "even if they did fall". 使 here makes a condition ("suppose"), not a causative (→ L6 n.7); later texts write 即使 or 縱使, and 即使 is still the modern word.

**有所 V** "have something that (one) V's": the opposite of 無所 (n. 2). 不能有所中傷 "could not hit or harm anything". **中** zhòng "to hit (the mark)", the verb, not zhōng "middle". Modern 中傷 means "to slander", a figurative "hit and hurt".

**奈 X 何** "what can be done about X?, what about X?": the thing in question goes *between* 奈 and 何. 奈地壞何 "what about the earth giving way?" Compare 奈何 in n. 9, where nothing stands in between. 如 X 何 works the same way: you'll meet it in L12 (如太形、王屋何).

**塊** kuài "clod of earth". **充塞** chōng sè "to fill up, stuff": 塞 read sè, "to block" (→ L10 n.2). 四虛 "the void in all four directions". The answer mirrors the first one point by point: 天，積氣耳 / 地積塊耳.

**躇步跐蹈** chú bù cǐ dǎo: four verbs of walking, "to stride, step, tread, stamp". The first answer had four for breathing and moving (屈伸呼吸): the man moves through heaven and stamps on earth all day without harm.

**舍然** shì rán "relieved, freed of worry" = 釋然: 舍 stands for 釋 "to let go" (a borrowed character, → L8 n.5), hence the reading shì. -然 makes it a description of manner (→ L3 n.3). 大喜 "greatly delighted".

glossary.en: Qi, a small state (in present-day Henan)
not to have, there is no (= 無)
to move about (lit. go and stop)

exercise.h: 偃之言是也，前言戲之耳。
exercise.py: Yǎn zhī yán shì yě, qián yán xì zhī ěr.
exercise.en: What Yan says is right; what I said before was only teasing him.
exercise.tests: 耳 = only; 是 here = right
exercise.h_s: 偃之言是也，前言戏之耳。

exercise.h: 既使我與若辯矣，若勝我，我不若勝，若果是也？我果非也邪？
exercise.py: Jì shǐ wǒ yǔ ruò biàn yǐ, ruò shèng wǒ, wǒ bù ruò shèng, ruò guǒ shì yě? Wǒ guǒ fēi yě yé?
exercise.en: Suppose you and I have argued. If you have beaten me and I have not beaten you, are you really right? Am I really wrong?
exercise.tests: 若 = you; 果; 邪; 使 = suppose; in 我不若勝 the pronoun object 若 comes before the verb, as it often does after a negative
exercise.h_s: 既使我与若辩矣，若胜我，我不若胜，若果是也？我果非也邪？

exercise.h: 亡而為有，虛而為盈，約而為泰，難乎有恆矣。
exercise.py: Wú ér wéi yǒu, xū ér wéi yíng, yuē ér wéi tài, nán hū yǒu héng yǐ.
exercise.en: Having nothing and acting as if one had, being empty and acting full, being poor and acting grand: it is hard for such a man to be constant.
exercise.tests: 亡 wú = 無, 虛, 而
exercise.h_s: 亡而为有，虚而为盈，约而为泰，难乎有恒矣。

exercise.h: 騅不逝兮可柰何！虞兮虞兮柰若何！
exercise.py: Zhuī bù shì xī kě nài hé! Yú xī Yú xī nài ruò hé!
exercise.en: My horse Zhui will not go on — what can be done? Yu, oh Yu, what will become of you?
exercise.tests: 柰 = 奈: 奈何, 奈 X 何, 若 = you (Xiang Yu's last song, to his lady Yu)
exercise.h_s: 骓不逝兮可柰何！虞兮虞兮柰若何！

lessons.culture: 杞人憂天 (or simply 杞憂, also borrowed into Japanese as *kiyū*) is said of anyone who frets about imaginary dangers. The *Liezi* goes on past our passage: a sage laughs at both men, and then Liezi himself laughs at the sage. Whether heaven and earth will perish, he says, "is not something I can know", so why trouble one's heart about it? The ending is pure Daoism: neither worry nor reassurance, but indifference.

lessons.title: 愚公移山（上）
lessons.title_en: The Foolish Old Man Moves the Mountains (1)

source.author: attributed to 列禦寇 Lie Yukou (Warring States); the text as we have it was edited by 張湛 (4th c. AD)
source.period: compiled by the 4th century AD from older material
source.text_from: 《列子·湯問》, first half (to 始一反焉). Words as in the 四部叢刊 text (Kanseki Repository KR5c0049), compared line by line, 2026-11-19, with the 四庫全書 文淵閣 text with 張湛's commentary (KR5c0125), the Hong Kong EDB recommended-passage edition (KS3-03) and the English Wiktionary citation (Citations:愚公移山, CC BY-SA). Punctuation follows Wiktionary and the EDB edition. Variants: 太形 (四部叢刊, 文淵閣, EDB; Wiktionary 太行; see n. 1); 丘 (文淵閣 邱, the Qing taboo form); 叩石 (文淵閣 即石); 獻疑曰 (EDB 疑之，曰); 箕畚運於 (EDB 以箕畚運於, Wiktionary 運于). The EDB text calls itself a reference version and modernises a few words; we follow the old editions.

lessons.intro: The longest story so far, and the most famous: Mao Zedong retold it in 1945, and every Chinese schoolchild learns it. The *Liezi* tells it among tales of the wonders at the edges of the world. It is long enough for two lessons; this one sets the scene and starts the work. New here: 汝 "you", 曾 zēng "even", 焉 as "where?" and at the end of a sentence, the fusion word 諸, and nouns and adjectives working as verbs (→ L10 n.10) on almost every line.

lines.en: The two mountains, Taihang and Wangwu,
were seven hundred li square
and ten thousand fathoms high.
They used to stand south of Jizhou
and north of Heyang.
The Foolish Old Man of North Mountain
was nearly ninety years old,
and lived facing the mountains.
Troubled that the mountains blocked the way to the north
and that going out and coming in took such a roundabout route,
he gathered his household to talk it over, saying:

lines.py: Wú yǔ rǔ bì lì píng xiǎn,
lines.en: "Let you and me put all our strength into levelling these steep heights,
lines.lit: I and you exhaust strength level steep

lines.en: open a way straight to the south of Yu,
reaching to the south bank of the Han:
shall we?"
They all agreed with him.
His wife raised a doubt:
"With your strength

lines.py: zēng bù néng sǔn Kuífù zhī qiū,
lines.en: you couldn't even make a dent in the hillock of Kuifu.
What could you do to Taihang and Wangwu?
And where would you put the earth and stones?"
They all said:
"We'll throw them at the far end of the Bohai,
north of Yintu."

lines.py: Suì shuài zǐ sūn hè dàn zhě sān fū,
lines.en: So he led those of his sons and grandsons who could carry a load, three men,
lines.lit: then led sons grandsons carry-load ones three men

lines.en: to break up the rocks and dig the soil,

lines.py: jī běn yùn yú Bóhǎi zhī wěi.
lines.en: and carried it in baskets to the far end of the Bohai.

lines.h: 鄰人京城氏之孀妻有遺男，
lines.py: Lín rén Jīngchéng shì zhī shuāng qī yǒu yí nán,
lines.en: The widow of their neighbour Jingcheng had a fatherless boy
lines.h_s: 邻人京城氏之孀妻有遗男，

lines.en: just losing his milk teeth;
he skipped along to help them.
Winter changed to summer
before they went home even once.

notes.text: **太形** is the 太行 Tàiháng range, which runs north–south between Shanxi and Hebei. The old editions write 形; 張湛's commentary says 形當作行 "形 should be 行", and Wiktionary and many modern editions print 太行. We keep the character of the old texts and give its own reading, xíng, but the mountains are the Taihang. **王屋** Wángwū "King's House" is a mountain in western Henan.

**方** "on each side, square" (→ L6 n.13). **仞** rèn, a man's height (seven or eight 尺), roughly "a fathom": 萬仞 "ten thousand fathoms" is simply "immensely high". Note the order: the subject (二山) and then two measurements with no verb, the noun-phrase predicate of → L8 n.2.

**本** běn "originally, at first" (古今詞義: the noun 本 is "root"; the adverb "originally" grew from it): the story explains why the mountains are no longer where they were. **冀州** Jìzhōu, one of the nine provinces of legend, in the north; **河陽** "north of the (Yellow) River". In place names, **陽** is the sunny side: north of a river, south of a mountain; **陰** is the shady side: south of a river, north of a mountain (漢陰 in line 14).

**Name + 者**: 北山愚公者 "(the one called) the Foolish Old Man of North Mountain". 者 after a noun marks it as the topic, the way a storyteller says "now, this old man …". It is not the 有 … 者 frame (→ L1 n.2), but it does the same job of bringing someone on stage. **公** gōng is a respectful word for an old man. 張湛 comments: 俗謂之愚者，未必非智也 "the one the world calls foolish is not necessarily unwise."
**且** qiě "nearly, about to" (→ L5 n.6) before a number: 年且九十 "(his) age (was) nearly ninety", with no verb (→ L8 n.2).
**面** miàn "face" used as a verb, "to face": 面山而居 "lived facing the mountains". A noun with an object becomes a verb (→ L10 n.10). 而 joins the manner to the main verb (→ L2 n.10).

**懲** chéng "to be troubled by, suffer from" (張湛 quotes 韓詩外傳: 懲，苦也). Modern 懲 is "to punish" (懲罰): 古今詞義. Its object is two subject + 之 + predicate phrases (→ L2 n.3): 山北之塞 "the north of the mountains' being blocked" and 出入之迂 "coming and going's being roundabout". **塞** is sè "to block" here (→ L10 n.2); **迂** yū "winding, roundabout".
**室** shì "household, family" (古今詞義: "room" is the root sense; the household is the people under one roof). 聚室而謀 "gathered his family and consulted": **謀** móu "to plan, deliberate".

**汝** rǔ "you", the plain second-person pronoun, to family and inferiors (→ L11 n.8, 若). It is also written 女 (read rǔ): 女與回也孰愈 (exercise 2). **畢力** "use up (our) strength": 畢 "to finish", so "all, entirely". **平險** "level the steep": the adjective 平 "flat" used as a verb meaning "make flat", the causative shift of → L10 n.10; 險 "steep" is a noun here, "the steep places".
**指** zhǐ "finger, to point" used as an adverb: "straight (as pointing)". 指通豫南 "open a way straight to the south of Yu" (豫 Yù, the province of present-day Henan).

**于 and 於.** Both are the preposition yú "at, to, in". 于 is the older spelling (the 詩經 and 書經 use it); Warring States prose prefers 於, but many texts mix them, like this one: 達**于**漢陰 here, 運**於**渤海之尾 in line 27. *Simplified-character warning:* simplified Chinese writes 于 for both, so 於 disappears (except as a surname); in traditional texts you'll see both. 漢陰 "south of the Han river" (n. 3).

**雜然** zá rán "all together, with one voice" (張湛: 雜猶僉也 "雜 means 'all'"); -然 → L3 n.3. **許** xǔ "to agree, consent". **相** here is not "each other" but "(to) him": 相許 "agreed with him". → L5 n.3 noted this one-way 相.
**獻** xiàn "to offer up (to a superior)": 獻疑 "raised a doubt", politely (張湛: 獻疑猶致難也 "raised an objection"). The wife is the only one to see the practical problem.

**君** jūn "lord" used for "you": a respectful second person, here a wife to her husband. Classical Chinese has a whole scale of "you": 君 and 子 (→ L2 n.7) polite, 若 (→ L11 n.8) and 汝 (n. 9) plain. 以君之力 "with your strength" (以 "with", → L1 n.10).

**曾** zēng "even, actually" before a negative: 曾不能 "couldn't even". Modern 曾 céng "once, ever" (曾經) is the same character in another word: in this story always read zēng. **損** sǔn "to reduce, damage". **魁父之丘** "the hillock of Kuifu", a tiny hill (張湛: 魁父，小山也).
**如 X 何** = 奈 X 何 (→ L11 n.15) "what can you do about X?": 如太形、王屋何 "what (could you do) to Taihang and Wangwu?" The wife's argument runs from small to big: not even a hillock, so how two mountains?

**焉** yān "where?": 焉置土石 "where (would you) put the earth and stones?" As a question word it stands before the verb (→ L9 n.11). **且** here is "moreover" (→ L5 n.6 mentions this sense). 置 "to put" (→ L9 n.2).

**諸** zhū = 之 + 於 run together, a fusion word (兼詞): 投諸渤海之尾 = 投之於渤海之尾 "throw them into the tail of the Bohai". The sound zhū is close to zhī + yú said fast. You will meet it constantly in the 論語: 求諸己 "seek it in oneself" (exercise 1). 渤海 the Bohai gulf; 隱土 Yintu, a place in the far north-east.

**率** shuài "to lead". **荷** hè "to carry on the shoulder" (hé "lotus" is the modern noun); **擔** dàn "a load on a carrying pole". **Numbers come after the noun**: 子孫荷擔者三夫 "sons and grandsons who could carry loads, three men". 夫 fū "a man (able-bodied adult)", not fú "now" (→ L2 n.9).
**叩** kòu "to knock, strike": 叩石 "broke the rocks" (the 四庫全書 copy has 即, a slip of the brush). **墾** kěn "to dig, break ground"; **壤** rǎng "soil".
**Nouns before the verb as instruments.** 箕 jī "winnowing basket" and 畚 běn "basket for earth" (張湛: 畚，籠也): 箕畚運 "carried (it) in baskets". The same shift as 廩食 (→ L8 n.6, L10 n.10).
**氏** shì "clan, family": 京城氏 "the Jingcheng family". **孀妻** "widow" (張湛: 孀，寡也); **遺男** "a son left behind" by his dead father: 遺 yí "to leave behind".

**始** shǐ "just, only just": 始齔 "just losing his milk teeth", about seven years old (張湛 quotes the 韓詩外傳 on children shedding their teeth at seven). The child and the old man of ninety work side by side.
**易** yì "to change, exchange" (the same character read yì means "easy", and 易 is also the *Book of Changes*). 寒暑易節 "cold and heat changed their season": a whole year went by.

**始** "only then" (n. 23 had "only just"); **反** = 返 "to go home" (→ L9 n.9). **焉** at the end of a sentence is often a fusion word like 諸 (n. 18): 於 + 之/是, "there, in it, from it". Here it has faded to a final particle rounding off the sentence ("only then did they go back, once"); in L13, 有子存焉 "there will be sons living (in the world)", the "there" is clear.

glossary.en: Jizhou, the northern province of legend
where?; (at the end) there, in it
cold and heat; winter and summer

exercise.h: 君子求諸己，小人求諸人。
exercise.py: Jūnzǐ qiú zhū jǐ, xiǎo rén qiú zhū rén.
exercise.en: The gentleman looks for it in himself; the small man looks for it in others.
exercise.tests: 諸 = 之於, 己 (→ L6 n.12)
exercise.h_s: 君子求诸己，小人求诸人。

exercise.h: 女與回也孰愈？
exercise.py: Rǔ yǔ Huí yě shú yù?
exercise.en: Which is the better, you or Hui?
exercise.tests: 女 = 汝 rǔ "you"; 孰 shú "which (of the two)?"
exercise.h_s: 女与回也孰愈？

exercise.h: 有事，弟子服其勞；有酒食，先生饌，曾是以為孝乎？
exercise.py: Yǒu shì, dìzǐ fú qí láo; yǒu jiǔ sì, xiānshēng zhuàn, zēng shì yǐ wéi xiào hū?
exercise.en: When there is work, the young do the toil; when there is wine and food, their elders are served: can that really be counted as filial piety?
exercise.tests: 曾 zēng; 以為 (→ L3 n.10); 食 sì "food"
exercise.h_s: 有事，弟子服其劳；有酒食，先生馔，曾是以为孝乎？

exercise.h: 眾惡之，必察焉；眾好之，必察焉。
exercise.py: Zhòng wù zhī, bì chá yān; zhòng hào zhī, bì chá yān.
exercise.en: When everyone hates a man, you must look into it; when everyone likes him, you must look into it.
exercise.tests: final 焉 = "into it"; 眾, 好 hào (惡 wù "to hate")
exercise.h_s: 众恶之，必察焉；众好之，必察焉。

lessons.culture: The places are real: the Taihang and Wangwu mountains stand between the Yellow River plain and the Shanxi plateau, and the story explains why the way south is open today. (The ending, in L13, tells who moved them.) On 11 June 1945 Mao Zedong closed the Seventh Party Congress with a speech called "The Foolish Old Man Who Removed the Mountains": the two mountains weighing on China, he said, are imperialism and feudalism, and "God" is the Chinese people.

lessons.title: 愚公移山（下）
lessons.title_en: The Foolish Old Man Moves the Mountains (2)

source.author: attributed to 列禦寇 Lie Yukou (Warring States); the text as we have it was edited by 張湛 (4th c. AD)
source.period: compiled by the 4th century AD from older material
source.text_from: 《列子·湯問》, second half (from 河曲智叟). Words as in the 四部叢刊 text (Kanseki Repository KR5c0049), compared line by line, 2026-11-19, with the 四庫全書 文淵閣 text with 張湛's commentary (KR5c0125), the Hong Kong EDB recommended-passage edition (KS3-03) and the English Wiktionary citation (Citations:愚公移山, CC BY-SA). Punctuation follows Wiktionary and the EDB edition. Variants: 夸娥 (文淵閣, EDB; 四部叢刊 and Wiktionary 夸蛾, see n. 19); 告之於 (Wiktionary 于); the EDB text reads 長歎, 我雖死 and 自是 for 長息, 雖我之死 and 自此, and Wiktionary has a slip, 汝心不固, for 汝心之固. Both old editions write 笑 in a variant form the transcriptions could not encode.

lessons.intro: The second half is an argument and a miracle. The Wise Old Man of the River Bend laughs at the project; the Foolish Old Man answers with the most famous speech in the *Liezi*, a chain of sons and grandsons that never ends. Watch the conjunction 雖 "even if", 其 as the subject of a clause and as a rhetorical "how ever", the inverted exclamation 甚矣，汝之不惠, and 已 meaning "to stop".

lines.py: Héqū Zhìsǒu xiào ér zhǐ zhī yuē:
lines.en: The Wise Old Man of the River Bend laughed and tried to stop him, saying:

lines.py: Shèn yǐ, rǔ zhī bù huì!
lines.en: "How great is your folly!
With the years and the strength you have left,

lines.py: zēng bù néng huǐ shān zhī yī máo,
lines.en: you can't even destroy a single hair of the mountain:
what can you ever do with all that earth and rock?"
The Foolish Old Man of North Mountain heaved a long sigh and said:
"The stubbornness of your mind
is past all getting through;

lines.py: zēng bù ruò shuāng qī ruò zǐ.
lines.en: you're not even as wise as the widow and her little boy.
Even if I die,
there will be my son left;
my son will father grandsons,
and the grandsons will father sons;
the sons will have sons,
and the sons will have grandsons:
sons and grandsons, generation after generation,
will never run out,
while the mountains will grow no bigger:
why fret that they won't be levelled?"
The Wise Old Man of the River Bend had no answer.

lines.py: Cāo shé zhī shén wén zhī,
lines.en: The snake-holding gods heard of it
and, afraid that he would never stop,
reported it to God on High.
God was moved by his sincerity

lines.py: mìng Kuā'é shì èr zǐ fù èr shān,
lines.en: and ordered the two sons of the Kua'e clan to carry off the two mountains on their backs,
one to be set down east of Shuo,
the other south of Yong.
From then on, south of Ji
and south of the Han,
there has been no ridge to bar the way.

notes.text: **河曲** "the bend of the (Yellow) River", where he lives; **智叟** "the Wise Old Man" (叟 sǒu "old man"). The two names are a pair, and the story turns them round: 張湛 comments 俗謂之智者，未必非愚也 "the one the world calls wise is not necessarily not a fool" (compare L12 n.4). **止之** "(tried to) stop him": 止 "to stop" (→ L4, 舟止) used with an object, "make (someone) stop", the causative shift of → L10 n.10.

**The predicate comes first** in an exclamation: 甚矣，汝之不惠 = 汝之不惠甚矣 "your lack of wisdom is extreme". Putting 甚矣 "(it is) extreme!" in front throws the weight on it, like English "How great is your folly!". 汝之不惠 is subject + 之 + predicate (→ L2 n.3). **惠** = 慧 huì "wise", a borrowed character (→ L8 n.5). You met the same shape in L3's exercise: 甚矣吾衰也.

**殘** cán "remaining, what is left over" (modern 殘 "cruel, damaged"); **餘** yú "surplus, remaining" (→ L5 n.4). *Simplified-character warning:* simplified Chinese writes 余 for 餘, and 余 is also the classical pronoun "I" (→ L3 n.6, 予 and 余). In a simplified classical text, 余 can be either word; the traditional text keeps them apart (mainland editions sometimes print 馀 where the two would clash).

**毀** huǐ "to destroy, demolish". **一毛** "a single hair": the trees and grass on a mountain are its hair. 曾不能 "can't even" (→ L12 n.15). The Wise Old Man repeats the wife's argument from L12, with contempt instead of concern.

**其 as a modal word**: before the verb of a question or a wish, 其 adds "how ever, surely": 其如土石何 "what *could* you ever do about the earth and rocks?" (如 X 何 → L12 n.16). So far 其 was "his, its" (→ L1 n.6) and "that" (→ L2 n.8); this 其 is an adverb. You met it in L3's exercise: 桓魋其如予何 "what can Huan Tui do to me?"
**息** xī "breath": 長息 cháng xī "a long breath, a deep sigh" (長 cháng "long", → L3 n.2). Modern 息 is mostly "rest" (休息) or "interest" (利息), both from "breathing (space)".

**Two 固 in a row.** 汝心之固 "the *solidness* of your mind", i.e. its obstinacy: the adjective 固 "solid, fixed" as a noun, in a subject + 之 + predicate phrase (→ L2 n.3). Then 固不可徹 "is *certainly* impenetrable": 固 "certainly" (→ L5 n.10). **徹** chè "to go right through".
**不若** "not as good as": 若 "to be like" (→ L4 n.7), so "not equal to". 曾不若孀妻弱子 "you are not even a match for the widow and her little boy" (L12 lines 28–30), who at least came to help.

**雖** suī "even if; although", the first conjunction in the course that introduces a whole clause. Here the clause is subject + 之 + predicate (→ L2 n.3): 雖我之死 "even granting my death". Whether 雖 is "although" (a fact) or "even if" (a supposition) depends on the context: the old man is still alive, so "even if". (L7's exercise had 雖令不從 "even if he gives orders, they are not followed".)
**存** cún "to survive, remain". **焉** = 於是 "in it, there" (→ L12 n.25): 有子存焉 "there will be sons remaining (in the world)".

**窮** qióng "to come to an end, be exhausted" (古今詞義: "poor" is 貧 in Classical Chinese; 窮 is to have come to the end of one's road). **匱** kuì "to run short". 無窮匱 "there will be no running out". 子子孫孫 "sons' sons and grandsons' grandsons": doubled nouns mean "one after another, every".
**而** "whereas, but": the contrast of → L1 n.9 between the endless family and the mountain that cannot grow. **加增** jiā zēng "to grow larger" (two words meaning "add, increase").

**何苦而不平** "what is there to worry about, that it won't be levelled?" 何苦 "what hardship, what is there to fret about" (modern 何苦 "why bother" comes from here). **平** "to be level" has a passive sense with no passive marker: the mountain "gets levelled". Classical Chinese often leaves the passive unmarked when the sense is clear (compare 可 + verb, → L1 n.8).
**亡以應** wú yǐ yìng = 無以應 "had nothing to answer with" (無以 → L8 n.11; 亡 read wú → L11 n.2). 應 "to answer" (→ L2 n.8). The wise man is beaten by the fool in argument before the gods step in.

**操蛇之神** "the snake-holding gods": a verb phrase + 之 + noun (→ L2 n.9), with 操 "to hold" (→ L9 n.7). 張湛 explains from the 山海經: the gods of the mountains and seas all hold snakes. The gods of these mountains are afraid of losing their home.

**其 as the subject of a clause.** 懼其不已 "feared his not stopping" = "feared that he would never stop". When a clause is the object of a verb (懼, 聞, 知 …), its subject is often 其 "his", the pronoun form of the "X 之" of → L2 n.3 (其 = 彼之 "his"). **已** yǐ "to stop, come to an end" (not "already", → L4 n.6): 不已 "not stop". The final 也 marks a pause (→ L6 n.2).

**告 A 於 B** "report A to B": 之 "it" (the matter) and 於帝 "to God". **帝** dì "the Lord on High", the supreme god of the sky (天帝 in L6); only from the First Emperor on did 帝 become the title of earthly rulers.
**感** gǎn "to be moved by"; **誠** chéng "sincerity, wholeheartedness" (a noun here; in L6 誠 was the adverb "truly", → L6 n.3). 其 "his" (→ L1 n.6).

**命 A V** "order A to V": like 使 (→ L6 n.7), 命 takes a person who then does the action. **夸娥氏** Kuā'é shì, a clan of giants or strong gods (張湛: "not in other records; probably gods of great strength"); the 四部叢刊 text and Wiktionary write 夸蛾. 二子 "two sons". **負** fù "to carry on the back".

**厝** cuò "to place, set down" (= 措 or 置). **一 … 一 …** "one … the other …". 朔東 "east of Shuo" (朔方, the far north) and 雍南 "south of Yong" (雍州, the far west): the mountains are moved to the edges of the world.
**自此** "from this (time) on": 自 "from" (→ L4 n.2), 此 "this". The story ends where it began, with an explanation of the landscape: 冀之南，漢之陰 (→ L12 n.3).

**隴斷** lǒng duàn (also written 壟斷) "a high ridge, a raised barrier": 無隴斷焉 "there was no barrier there" (焉 → n. 10). Mencius has the same word, written 龍斷, for the high mound from which a greedy trader looked over the whole market to corner it; that is where modern 壟斷 "monopoly" comes from (古今詞義).

glossary.en: the bend of the Yellow River
(in questions) how ever, surely; (subject of a clause) he
what is there to worry about?
to stop, come to an end
